Article
The Global Pact for the Environment: Freshwater
and Economic Law Synergies
Brian McGarry*
ABSTRACT
The Global Pact for the Environment has been proposed as an overarching framework
for international environmental law, which would solidify and advance this regime
in light of pressing challenges and the demands of the UN Sustainable Development
Goals. By codifying principles in legally binding form, the Global Pact has attracted high
expectations that it can bridge normative gaps in international environmental law and
environment-related instruments, such as trade and investment agreements. The present
article scrutinizes this prospect by treating the management of freshwater as a case study
for the Global Pact’s potential success. The article first identifies key interplays between
sources of international water law and rules governing international economic law. It
then indicates how the Global Pact might effectively minimize or resolve lacunae in the
convergenceoftheseregimeswithoutunderminingexistinginstrumentsandframeworks.
The author concludes that the proposed form of the Global Pact is a promising means to
clarify normative interactions between freshwater management and international trade
and investment, while accelerating and broadening the implementation of environmental
principles within these domains.

I. REGIME INTERPLAYS
A. Legal context for the Global Pact in the management of freshwater
Current international law largely aims to protect freshwater resources through a patch-
work of global, regional, and basin agreements, with certain general principles and
customary rules applicable to gaps therein. The need for comprehensive legal rules
to govern the protection of this resource is underscored by its status as a vital ele-
ment of human health and welfare.9 Among the long-standing threats to the human
consumption of freshwater, contamination of water sources through chemical and
industrial pollutants particularly threatens developing States and water-scarce areas.10
Additionally, the degradation of water quality poses a critical threat to biodiversity and
the conservation of water-based ecosystems, which may suffer due to the introduction
of invasive species in rivers and lakes11 and alterations in precipitation and groundwater
recharge due to deforestation.12

1. Regulatory framework of international water law
The UNWC is the global treaty that most directly governs the uses of freshwater.
Recalling UN Charter Article 1(3) (which applies the principle of cooperation to
the context of ‘international problems of an economic’ character) and Articles 2 and
13(1)(a) thereof—as well as the principles and recommendations adopted in the 1992
Rio Declaration and Agenda 21—the UNWC’s Preamble ‘express[es] the conviction
that a framework convention will ensure the utilization, development, conservation,
management and protection of international watercourses and the promotion of the
optimal and sustainable utilization thereof for present and future generations’. The
UNWC seeks this goal through several provisions establishing broad duties for States
in respect of freshwater governance, such as duties of cooperation (Article 8) and
environmental democracy through access to information (Article 9).13
The transversal nature of freshwater as an object of legal regulation is seen in the
patchwork of other treaties and instruments governing aspects of its use, which differ
substantially in their focus. This spectrum of treaties includes multilateral environmen-
tal agreements of a universal scope, such as the 2015 Paris Agreement. Further diversity
of obligations relating to freshwater arises in a range of binding regional or basin-level
instruments. Such treaties include European agreements such as the 1999 Convention
on the Protection of the Rhine, African agreements such as the 2008 Niger Basin
Water Charter, Asian agreements such as the 1995 Agreement on the Cooperation
for the Sustainable Development of the Mekong River Basin, and bilateral treaties in
the Americas such as the 1972 Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement. While some
treatiesgoverningfreshwatermaycodifyoroperationalizegeneralprinciplesrelevantto
environmental protection,14 this patchwork is also supplemented by a number of non-
binding instruments that aim to codify or progressively develop customary rules at the
universal level,15 such as UN Sustainable Development Goal 6.16

2. Normative and institutional gaps
In spite of the aforementioned provisions, the UNWC is insufficient as a global gover-
nance mechanism for the protection of freshwater resources. As a preliminary matter,
the UNWC expressly excludes from its scope ‘[t]he uses of international watercourses
fornavigation’.17 Acknowledgingthemanyconnectionsbetweennavigationandthepro-
tection of watercourses, the International Law Commission (ILC) recognized that ‘the
exclusion of navigational uses from the scope of the [UNWC] cannot be complete’.18
Vessel-source pollution of freshwater thus falls within a multifaceted arrangement of
legal regimes, giving rise to normative gaps.
Secondly, as a framework treaty, the UNWC’s prescriptions are inherently broad
and sometimes hortatory. This ensures flexibility for States to adopt implementing
agreements in respect of individual watercourses, but in so doing sacrifices the benefits
ofmorespecificguidanceastotheresultingformoffreshwaterprotection.19 Specifically,
despite Article 3’s aspirations,20 the UNWC does not provide any binding directives as
to the establishment of joint enforcement or dispute settlement mechanisms, in order
to see that the principle of equitable and reasonable utilization is given effect.21 Article
6’s list of factors to be assessed in this utilization is non-exhaustive, leaving to States the
difficult task of reaching subsequent agreement as to specific factors applicable in the
use of their shared watercourses.22
The interaction of provisions such as Articles 6 and 7 (‘Obligation not to cause
significant harm’) of the UNWC is to be interpreted with due regard to the develop-
ment of international environmental law. Customary principles and rules relating to
environmental protection may clarify, organize, and define the meaning, substance,
and scope of the rights and obligations established by water agreements, as well as
supplement those rights and obligations. Accounting for the relevant legal context may
allowanadaptiveanddynamicinterpretationandapplicationofwateragreements.23 Yet
it must be borne in mind that this analytical process arises directly from the fragmented
characterofthecurrentframeworkoffreshwatergovernanceandtheneedtofilllacunae
resulting from this relative lack of legal integration.
Themyriadgapsinthecurrentmosaicofbindingandsoft-lawinstrumentsrelatedto
the protection of freshwater resources are further complicated by the multidirectional
manner in which these instruments interact. While the lacunae in the UNWC may
be supplemented by subsequent agreements between riparian States, so too may the
UNWC serve to fill gaps in existing agreements between these States.24 Ambiguity in

B. Contemporary links with international economic law
BeyondtheUNWC’splacementof ‘[t]hesocialand economicneedsof thewatercourse
States concerned’, among factors relevant to equitable and reasonable utilization of
international watercourses,27 its travaux préparatoires include several express provisions
that emphasize economic interests in the interpretation of the UNWC’s applicable law.
These include references to the need for cooperation in light of growing economic,
environmental, and physical interdependencies;28 the trifurcation and characterization
of potential uses as ‘industrial, economic or private’;29 harmonious uses of terms and
principles in the Charter of Economic Rights and Duties of States;30 the potential
provision of monetary compensation as an ‘equitable resolution’;31 and other legal
instruments calling for greater economic utilization of hydrographic basins and streams
for the production of electric power.32
While the UNWC appears to have a long road to universal adoption, a holistic
view of State obligations may require a State’s adherence to norms embodied in the
UNWC in light of its accession to related instruments of international economic law.33
Reciprocally, international economic norms can complement and find application in
the UNWC.34 Indeed, the UNWC is one of several treaties that address water issues

1. Key aspects of international trade for water resources governance
a. Interactions within the WTO system

Notably, factors such as increased agricultural production imply that instruments such

Although the non-discrimination obligations of Articles I, III, and XIII of the GATT
are potentially applicable to State measures affecting international watercourses, Article
XI’s broad prohibition against quantitative restrictions may be particularly relevant to
bulk water exports, since it could be construed as restricting WTO Member States from
enacting laws or policies that regulate these exports.44 Notably, such non-tariff measures
governed by the GATT are subject to general exceptions under GATT Article XX that
may be relevant to norms reflected in the UNWC. These exceptions have not been
directly applied to a dispute concerning trade in water, although at least one such WTO
proceeding was initiated through a request for consultations.45 In particular, measures
concerning freshwater in its natural state could be considered ‘necessary to protect
human, animal or plant life or health’ or ‘relating to the conservation of exhaustible nat-
ural resources’ within the meaning of GATT Articles XX(b) and XX(g), respectively.46
The first of these exceptions is further elaborated in the Agreement on the Applica-
tion of Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures. If policies designed to prevent domestic
water scarcity include freshwater export restrictions, such restrictions can arguably
be justified under this exception.47 The second exception could arguably justify poli-
cies designed to protect domestic water resources that include export restrictions
on exhaustible flows of water.48 Two specific cases may be helpful in reaching some
precision regarding the scope of this exception vis-à-vis international watercourses.

B. Accelerating implementation through decentralization
Implementation of the Global Pact would require that its principles be transduced into
State-level laws and regulations, and the monitoring of their application entails the con-
sideration of both legal and economic factors.109 A large majority of States have already
incorporated generically formulated environmental principles into their constitutions
since the 1972 Stockholm Declaration, with some going further in codifying more
specificconstitutionalprovisionsincludingtherightofaccesstowater.110 Constitutional
courts have thus far played a critical role in implementing these principles in disputes
involving large-scale economic interests. The Constitutional Courts of Ecuador and
Latvia have identified breaches of the right to a healthy environment in cases involving
industrialproductionandlanddevelopment,respectively,withthelatterreferencingthe
Stockholm Declaration and Aarhus Convention in elaborating on this principle.111 The
Supreme Court of Chile inferred the same constitutional right in a dispute involving a
major logging project, which itself was subsequently the focus of a finding by the Inter-
American Commission on Human Rights of a breach of environmental democracy
principles (specifically access to information).112 In another timber-clearing dispute, the
Supreme Court of the Philippines inferred from the constitutional right to a healthy
environment the corollary principle of intergenerational responsibility.113 In a case
involving pollution of the atmosphere and the cultural preservation of the Taj Mahal,
the Supreme Court of India issued a sweeping edict mixing constitutional analysis with
three principles sourced from international law (precautionary principle, the polluter-
pays principle, and the principle of sustainable development).114
The protection of freshwater resources has provided no less opportunity for this
symbiotic relationship between the reasoning of national courts and the crystallization
of such principles within the framework of international law. Foundational environ-
mental law cases in Canada and the United States set the stage for such developments
in that region in disputes involving hydroelectric projects on major rivers.115 In a saga
drawing upon principles of sustainable development and intergenerational responsibil-
ity, Greece’s Council of State (its supreme administrative court) ruled against a large-
scale irrigation and energy project in the Acheloos River, following an opinion from the
Court of Justice of the European Union expressing concerns regarding the water diver-

The approach of these courts and tribunals is consistent with the gap-filling func-
tion of general principles, as a treaty cannot through silence preclude the potential
application of subsequently emergent principles.125 The same conclusion can thus
be drawn as concerns economic instruments that expressly incorporate principles of
international law by general reference. For example, in one of the investment cases to
emerge from the Libyan crude oil dispute in the 1970s, a contractual clause provided
that the concession agreements may only be subject to the provisions of Libyan law
so long as they are ‘common to the principles of international law and in the absence
of such common principles then by and in accordance with the general principles

III. CONCLUSION
A watercourse that is utilized in an environmentally unsustainable manner is destined
to become economically unsustainable as well.135 In particular, the incorporation of
sustainable development principles within the UNWC implicitly raises challenges to
maintain balance among its non-hierarchical system of economic and environmental
watercourse uses. Indeed, the principle of sustainability might be said to limit the
freedom of States to balance interests, thus enjoying a position of priority by joining
economic and environmental uses.136 For example, such a balance may be achieved by
considering both the ‘legitimate interests’ of a foreign investor and those of environ-
mental protection under the circumstances.137 The Global Pact provides opportunities
to calibrate this balance by drawing inspiration from trade and investment law to sup-
plement gaps in the freshwater regime, such as the UNWC’s prohibition of nationality-
baseddiscriminationingrantingaccesstojudicialandotherprocedures,whichdoesnot
clearly impose a duty to develop these procedures at a level sufficient to protect public
participation and provide access to remedies.138

as a ‘third generation’ of fundamental rights, following the International Covenant on
Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and
Cultural Rights.139 Distinguishing the Global Pact in this manner undercuts one of its
central functions: to recognize and normatively manage the existing interrelations of
